reading.rtitle: Halfway There: Why Adult Learners Stall in the Middle
paras: Ask any language teacher about the middle of a course and you will hear the same word: plateau. In the first months, progress is easy to see. You learn a new tense, you use it the next day, and you can feel the difference. Then, somewhere around the halfway point, the curve flattens. Having learned the basics, most adults stop noticing their own progress, and many quietly assume they have stopped improving.

They have not, but something real has changed. At the start, every lesson added something new. In the middle, the gains are finer: fewer fillers, faster answers, a tense used without thinking. The more advanced you are, the harder your progress is to see, and the easier it is to backslide into a comfort zone, falling back on the few structures you already trust.

Researchers who study adult learners say the way out is not more hours but deliberate practice. That means pinpointing one sticking point, such as the tense you avoid or the sound you swallow, and working on it on purpose, with feedback. One learner described his breakthrough like this: he was going to quit in his tenth month, but he had his recordings analyzed by a teacher instead, and found three habits he had never noticed.

The final advice is about consistency. Twenty focused minutes, four times a week, is nowhere near as impressive as a weekend course, but it works far better. Self-aware learners also do one more thing at the midpoint: they raise the bar. Instead of asking whether they can survive a conversation, they ask whether they can control it.

bank.label: Useful language for an honest progress audit
items: Having finished half the course, I can see real progress.
The more I speak, the less I translate in my head.
I was going to skip the recordings, but I am glad I did not.
I had my last presentation recorded, and I noticed three fillers.
My listening is nowhere near as good as my speaking yet.
My sticking point is the past perfect. I tend to avoid it.
For the second half, I want to raise the bar.

lf.text: A and D, in blue, are the FUTURE IN THE PAST (lesson 21): a plan or a moment that was coming, seen from the past, often one that did not happen. B is the CAUSATIVE (lesson 18): somebody else did it for me. C is a PARTICIPLE CLAUSE (lesson 20): HAVING + past participle replaces 'Because she has lived'. Ask yourself first: was it a plan, a service, or a reason?

items: Describe your English twelve months ago and today. Use 'nowhere near as ... as' and 'the more ... the more'.
Tell one plan that changed: something you were going to do this year and did not, and why.
Name one sticking point in your English and say how you will work on it with deliberate practice.
A colleague says: 'I think I have stopped improving.' Answer with a short reply first ('I don't think so'), then give advice.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
list: Gap-fill: 1 = backslide, 2 = comfort zone, 3 = deliberate practice, 4 = pinpoint, 5 = sticking point, 6 = consistency.
Model (Scenario 1): 'A year ago my listening was nowhere near as fast as it is now. The more podcasts I hear, the less I need subtitles.'
Model (Scenario 2): 'I was going to do a course in Dublin in July, but the new warehouse opened and I had to stay.'
Model (Scenario 3): 'My sticking point is the present perfect. For the next month, I will write three sentences with it every morning and have them checked.'
Model (Scenario 4): 'I don't think so. Having heard you last month, I can tell you are much faster now.'
answerkey.note: A review is not a test of memory. If one structure did not come out, that is your sticking point for the second half: write it down.

listenings.text: Hi Marcelo, it is Fiona again. I hope the debate after my last column did not keep you up at night. I have a new idea, and I would love your help. My editor wants a piece on adults who learn a language in the middle of a busy career. Having interviewed three teachers already, I need one learner who is honest about it, not a success story. I was going to ask a friend of mine, but she has only just started, and I want someone who is halfway. Could you give me twenty minutes on Thursday? I want to know three things. What has changed since you started, what your sticking point is now, and what you would tell someone who is about to give up. Let me know if Thursday works for you.

Welcome back to The Long Game, the podcast about learning things the slow way. Today, the plateau. Every serious learner hits it, and most of them misread it. They think the plateau means they have stopped. It does not. It means the easy gains are over. When you start, every week brings something new and visible. In the middle, progress becomes small and quiet, a little less hesitation here, one more idiom there. The trap is what people do next. Some quit. Others go back to their comfort zone and use the same twenty sentences forever. The learners who break through do something different. They record themselves, they pinpoint one problem, and they work on that problem, and only that problem, for a month. It is boring, and it works. So if you feel stuck this week, do not add more hours. Choose one thing, and fine-tune it.

extra_audio.text: First, I say how much of the course I have finished. Then, I say what has changed since I started. After that, I pinpoint my sticking point. Next, I explain how I will work on it with deliberate practice. Finally, I raise the bar for the second half.
